title: Becoming Jane
full_review:
How autobiographical are the novels of Jane Austen?

"Becoming Jane" (Miramax) takes the few known facts about an episode in the 18th-century author's life and concocts a romantic escapade with strong parallels to those classic works to demonstrate how she may have gotten her inspiration.

Twenty-year-old Austen (Anne Hathaway), already hoping to be a novelist, lives in somewhat humble circumstances with her parents, the Rev. George Austen (James Cromwell) and mother Cassandra (Julie Walters), in rural Hampshire. As the reverend is having serious financial difficulties, they have their calculating eye on Mr. Wisley (Laurence Fox), the wealthy but dull nephew of imperious Lady Gresham (Maggie Smith), as a match for their bookish daughter.

Wisley proposes, but Jane doesn't love him, and withholds an immediate answer. Her mother warns her she'll be an "old maid" and that money is indispensable. The reverend agrees. "Nothing destroys spirit like poverty," he counsels her.

The household also includes Jane's sister, Cassandra (Anna Maxwell Martin), and brother, Henry (Joe Anderson), who's back from Oxford with a friend, Tom Lefroy (James McAvoy), in tow.

When Jane meets this handsome but impecunious Irish lawyer from Limerick, she recognizes a kindred spirit, once they get over some early sparring, that is, like so many Austen heroines.

Tom's benefactor, his severe uncle, Judge Langlois (the late Ian Richardson in his last role), whom we see sentence a man to hanging, vehemently opposes any union between his nephew and Jane, when he learns of it through an anonymous letter. What will they do?

Julian Jarrold ("Kinky Boots") -- working from Sarah Williams and Kevin Hood's not quite witty enough script -- directs with an authentic 18th-century feel, and performances are good, with American Hathaway holding her own reasonably well among such British acting pros, though truth to tell her British accent is sometimes dicey.

The film itself is a mixed bag. Just as the cinematography and production design seem lovely in spots, dank in others, the film is somehow not entirely satisfying, though it nonetheless holds your interest right up to its bittersweet ending.

Though possibly acceptable for older teens, the film contains a couple of boxing sequences, a frisky but nongraphic husband and wife encounter, some prostitutes, an implied premarital encounter, mild innuendo and brief sexual allusions. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
